brief:

label: Idle-read watchdog, go-containerregistry retried writes, and the dist CDN user agent
brief:
Revision of go-network.md (GO-NET), holding every ID stable. GO-NET-06's streaming branch is a MUST with no fixture, GO-NET-17 tells CLIs to wrap a retry path nobody watched, and GO-NET-18 waits on one probe.
(1) GO-NET-06 streaming branch. Write the smallest correct idle-read watchdog for a blob-streaming client: a reader wrapper that resets a time.AfterFunc on every Read returning n>0 and cancels the request context through context.WithCancelCause with a typed stall cause, on a transport cloned from http.DefaultTransport with ResponseHeaderTimeout set and Client.Timeout 0. Fixture in /home/mherwig/.cache/research-lang/go-tools/fixtures/go-network-stall/: one httptest server sends headers and 4 KiB then stalls; a second trickles 1 byte per 100 ms for 3 s. Red: without the watchdog the read blocks until the test's own deadline. Green: the stall fails within the idle bound carrying the typed cause, and the trickle completes. Read go1.27.1 src/net/http/transport.go for any built-in body idle deadline, compare a per-Read SetReadDeadline conn wrapper, and pick one shape.
(2) go-containerregistry retry. Read google/go-containerregistry@0c8bedb78437 pkg/v1/remote/transport/retry.go:95-115 and pkg/v1/remote/options.go:95-104,179. Plant an httptest registry (or ggcr pkg/registry wrapped by a handler) that answers the first PATCH or PUT of a blob upload with 503 and then succeeds; run remote.Write of a random layer through a GO-NET-03 transport. Record whether the retried request carries the full body, an empty body, or fails; whether the discarded 503 response body is closed (count connections); what remote.WithRetryStatusCodes and remote.WithRetryBackoff change.
(3) GO-NET-18. Request the ocx bootstrap asset URL used by /home/mherwig/dev/ocx-sdk-python/src/ocx_sdk/_dist.py (setup.ocx.sh) with User-Agent Go-http-client/1.1, the Python-urllib default and ocx-sdk-go/0.0.0; record the status codes. If the network is unreachable, record not measured.
Decide: GO-NET-06's streaming clause text and a watched verification; whether GO-NET-17 gains a fourth go-containerregistry gap and its mitigation; GO-NET-18's severity.

group_label: Language era, modernization and stdlib semantics (GO-LANG)
label: Generics and iterator design: when a type parameter earns its place, constraints, and writing iter.Seq correctly
brief:
Revision of go-language.md (GO-LANG), holding every ID stable; new rules continue the sequence. The orchestrator's self-direction sweep found generics and iterator DESIGN nearly absent from the corpus (go-api.md has zero rows on type parameters or iter.Seq; go-language.md covers era idioms, not design). This is a load-bearing gap for Go expertise: LLM-written Go characteristically over-generalizes, mis-states constraints, and writes iterators that break the range-over-func contract.
Fetch and read in full: the spec sections on type parameters, type sets, core types (and the Go 1.25 removal of core types from the spec: go.dev/blog/coretypes), go.dev/doc/tutorial/generics, go.dev/blog/when-generics, go.dev/blog/intro-generics, go.dev/blog/range-functions, go.dev/blog/generic-interfaces (2025), the iter package doc (pkg.go.dev/iter: Seq, Seq2, Pull, Pull2 and the naming conventions it states: All, Backward, Keys, Values), the Go 1.23 release notes on range-over-func, the Go 1.24 generic type alias notes, the Go 1.26/1.27 notes on self-referential generics, and the cmp, slices, maps packages' generic signatures (why slices.Sort takes S ~[]E).
Pin down with planted fixtures under fixtures/generics-and-iterators/, each watched: (a) an iterator that ignores yield's return value (for i := range n { yield(i) }): record the exact runtime panic text when the consumer breaks early, and whether any vet analyzer, staticcheck check or golangci linter flags it statically (search the analyzer lists; plant and run go vet, staticcheck -checks all, golangci-lint with default: all on a scratch config outside the fixture); (b) iter.Pull without calling stop: goroutine leak? measure with runtime.NumGoroutine and goleak; (c) a function with a type parameter used once that should take an interface or a concrete type (is there any linter? if none, it is a reading heuristic); (d) constraints: any vs comparable (the 1.20 comparable relaxation and its runtime panic on interface keys), ~T approximation elements, cmp.Ordered vs a hand-rolled Number constraint including floats and NaN ordering, constraints.Ordered from golang.org/x/exp (superseded, flag as depguard entry?); (e) methods cannot have type parameters: the compile error text and the idiomatic workaround (a generic function taking the receiver); (f) generic type alias usage and gopls/vet support.
Measure in the exemplar corpus (non-test, non-generated, per repo): type-parameter declarations by kind (func vs type), how many generic functions have exactly one instantiation in-repo (heuristic acceptable, state FP rate), iter.Seq/Seq2 returning functions and how many ignore yield's result (grep 'yield(' lines not inside an if or return; spot-read 20), iter.Pull uses and whether stop is deferred. Name the best exemplar iterators (e.g. golang/tools, tailscale) with citations.
Decide: when a library or the SDK exports a generic API (default from the owner: the SDK exports slices, not iter.Seq; keep it), the rule text for yield-checking (MUST, with the runtime panic as rationale and the best verification you can watch), iter.Pull stop discipline, constraint choice, naming (All/Keys/Values/Backward), and which agent mistakes to list. label: Performance hygiene: benchmarks that measure, allocation evidence, PGO, and when not to optimize
brief:
Revision of go-observability.md (GO-OBS), holding every ID stable; new rules continue the sequence. The map deferred M-J-07 (PGO) and M-J-09 (allocation hygiene) as outside the named consumers; the orchestrator's self-direction sweep promotes them, because performance advice is where LLM-written Go is most confidently wrong (premature sync.Pool, fmt.Sprintf in hot loops, unfounded 'X% faster' claims from one run, pointer-receiver-everywhere for 'speed'). GO-TEST-19 (b.Loop, benchstat) exists: cite it, do not restate it.
Fetch and read in full: go.dev/doc/pgo (default.pgo in the main package dir, -pgo=auto default since 1.21, merging profiles, what it cannot do for libraries), go.dev/doc/gc-guide (GOGC, GOMEMLIMIT, the Green Tea GC default in 1.26), go.dev/doc/diagnostics, the golang.org/x/perf/cmd/benchstat README (-count >= 10 guidance, significance, geomean), go.dev/blog/pgo and pgo-preview, the compiler's escape analysis docs (go build -gcflags=-m, -m=2; go.dev/wiki/CompilerOptimizations), the sync.Pool doc (its stated use cases and the 'do not use for short-lived objects' guidance), strings.Builder, slices.Grow/make with capacity, bytes.Buffer, the prealloc and perfsprint linters' docs, and one or two authoritative practitioner posts (e.g. Dave Cheney high performance Go workshop, Go blog profiling posts).
Pin down with planted fixtures under fixtures/performance-hygiene/, each watched: (a) perfsprint on fmt.Sprintf("%d", n) and string concatenation: does the linter flag it, and does benchstat on a b.Loop benchmark show a significant difference at -count=10 (record the benchstat table); (b) prealloc: a slice appended in a loop of known length, and whether the linter is noise on the eight standard exemplars (ko, cobra, oras-go, zap, go-cmp, regclient, fzf, urfave/cli; hits per 10k LOC, hand-classified sample); (c) escape analysis: show -gcflags=-m output for returning a pointer to a local vs a value and an interface conversion that allocates; (d) a sync.Pool misuse (pooling a small struct) vs correct use (large byte buffers), benchmarked; (e) PGO: build a small CLI with and without default.pgo from a CPU profile and record whether the binary changes and whether a benchmark moves, with benchstat; (f) testing.AllocsPerRun or b.ReportAllocs as an allocation regression test.
Measure in the exemplar corpus: default.pgo files committed (which repos), sync.Pool usage counts, perfsprint and prealloc enablement in the 23 golangci configs.
Decide: which performance rules are MUST (probably few: evidence before optimization claims, no benchmark conclusion from one run, AllocsPerRun guard where allocation is the contract), which are SHOULD or CONSIDER, whether perfsprint/prealloc join the fleet config (feed the answer to GO-GATE via a cross-family note; do not edit go-gates.md), the PGO stance for CLIs vs libraries, and the ranked agent mistakes.
